Devis (Encrasicholina devisi) is a small, fast-growing engraulid species that dominates coastal pelagic fish assemblages in the tropical Indo-Pacific. Females release pelagic, yolk-laden eggs that measure approximately 0.8 millimeters in diameter, and from this egg size the wet weight at birth has been calculated at 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams]. The incubation period is remarkably brief: under the stable thermal regime typical of its tropical habitat, maintained at 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], embryogenesis is completed and yolk-sac larvae emerge after just 3 days [ab = 3 days]. This rapid hatching is consistent with the high metabolic rates and accelerated developmental schedules observed in small-bodied tropical clupeiforms, where rapid progression through the vulnerable yolk-sac stage reduces the window of exposure to planktonic predators. The lecithotrophic larvae, still dependent upon their endogenous yolk reserves, commence exogenous feeding shortly thereafter, transitioning to a zooplanktivorous diet as soon as the mouth gapes and retinal differentiation permit effective prey detection.

Growth proceeds at a vigorous pace during the pelagic larval and juvenile phases, reflecting the warm environmental conditions. Field surveys indicate that Devis attains sexual maturation at a total length of 6.1 centimeters [Lp = 6.1 centimeters], a size that is typically reached within a few months of hatching. Correspondingly, body mass at the onset of puberty is estimated at 1.99 grams [Wwp = 1.99 grams], derived from the allometric relationship between length and weight. This pubertal size threshold is quite small relative to many other engraulids, underscoring the species' opportunistic, r-selected life-history strategy. The ability to mature rapidly and at a modest body size allows Devis to capitalize on ephemeral pulses of primary and secondary productivity in coastal upwelling zones. Individuals that survive the intense predation pressure characteristic of the planktonic environment can therefore quickly contribute to the next generation, a trait that stabilizes local populations despite high natural mortality rates among early life stages.

Adult Devis continue to grow after the onset of reproduction, eventually reaching an ultimate total length of 9.7 centimeters [Li = 9.7 centimeters], which represents the maximum size attained by this species. The corresponding ultimate wet weight is 8 grams [Wwi = 8 grams], reflecting the slender, fusiform body plan typical of anchovies. This final body size is modest even by engraulid standards and is linked to the species' relatively brief lifespan. Under the prevailing environmental conditions of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], maximum recorded longevity in wild populations is approximately 620 days [am = approximately 620 days]. This short lifespan, combined with rapid maturation and elevated reproductive output, positions Devis as an archetypal fast-lived small pelagic fish, heavily reliant on high fecundity to offset the substantial mortality incurred throughout its life cycle. Senescence appears to set in quickly after the first year of life, with very few individuals surviving beyond the second year in nature. The species achieves a maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 29 to 30 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 29 to 30 eggs per day] when water temperatures remain at the optimal 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C].

Despite the brevity of its life, Devis exhibits a remarkable capacity for population increase, driven by continuous spawning activity throughout the year in tropical waters. At a stable temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], gravid females release approximately 29 to 30 eggs per day. When expressed in terms of clutch-based metrics, this translates into an average fecundity of roughly 29 to 30 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 29 to 30 eggs per spawning event], with females spawning approximately once per day under optimal thermal conditions [F_R_i = spawning approximately once per day under optimal thermal conditions]. This nearly continuous reproductive schedule is facilitated by the rapid vitellogenesis and oocyte maturation enabled by the warm environment. The resulting daily reproductive output is among the highest recorded for any clupeiform of this body size, allowing Devis to compensate for the high mortality rates experienced by its pelagic eggs and larvae. Such prodigious fecundity is a critical adaptation for a species that faces intense predation from a wide array of piscivorous fishes, cephalopods, and seabirds throughout its range.

Comparisons with congeneric species reveal that Devis occupies an extreme position along the fast-slow life-history continuum within the genus Encrasicholina. Its pubertal length of 6.1 centimeters [Lp = 6.1 centimeters] is substantially smaller than that of the closely related Encrasicholina heteroloba, which matures at over 7 centimeters, while the ultimate length of 9.7 centimeters [Li = 9.7 centimeters] is also at the lower end of the genus range. The associated wet weight at puberty of 1.99 grams [Wwp = 1.99 grams] and the ultimate wet weight of 8 grams [Wwi = 8 grams] reflect this diminutive stature. At the population level, these life-history traits, combined with a lifespan of approximately 620 days [am = approximately 620 days] at 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C] and a birth mass of just 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], generate a demographic profile characterized by rapid turnover and high resilience to fishing pressure. The species' ability to sustain such high reproductive rates despite a brief lifespan underscores the efficiency of its energy acquisition and allocation strategies in productive tropical coastal ecosystems, where it serves as a critical trophic link between zooplankton and higher-level predators.
